claims.statement: The documented Sesam project lifecycle uses API features with external development tools for version control, local/CI testing, and optional automatic deployment rather than a built-in project configuration-management suite.

The Sesam client is documented to download and upload JSON configuration, simulate pipe runs from start to finish, and compare actual with expected outputs; installation and usage are handed off to the external sesam-community/sesam-py README.
The client is intended for personal testing subscriptions and dedicated CI/CD testing subscriptions, and its documentation explicitly warns not to run it on production subscriptions.
Only one client instance may run commands on a subscription at a time, and manual changes while the client runs are warned against because they can produce undesired results.

The environment guide separates per-developer development subscriptions, a CI-test subscription, a production-sized test subscription, and production, and recommends test data for all incoming data types so developers can test independently before propagation.

Documented local testing requires output pipes to be disabled or unable to send to their systems; CI must be unable to write to another system and should not contain the variables or secrets needed for usual output connections.
Disabling a pump prevents automatic execution but still permits a manual start, so pump disablement alone is not an absolute output-write barrier.

Conditional sources and sinks select an alternative using a key typically controlled by an environment variable, resolve the selected component when the parent pipe is created, and require every possible condition value to be present in alternatives.

The documented development isolation pattern uses conditional sources for anonymized embedded inputs and conditional sinks with a development null alternative; a null sink discards written entities and does nothing rather than writing to an external destination.
An embedded source stores input entities inside source configuration and is intended for small, static datasets, not a large number of entities.

The version-control guide recommends exporting configuration through the client, API, or portal into a VCS working copy, including pipes, systems, expected, and variables directories, and using GitHub Flow with semantic-version release tags.

Sesam retains uploaded pipe/system configuration versions in system:config and exposes previous configurations, but the guide explicitly says this history is not proper project version control and recommends a separate VCS.

The documented default endpoint-test contract places expected beside pipes and systems and requires a <name_of_pipe>.json expected-result file plus a <name_of_pipe>.test.json test-configuration file for each endpoint pipe.

Test configuration offers optional naming/type/description, pipe selection, and expected-file selection; foo.test.json defaults to foo.json, while the authored pipe-default description repeats the expected-file wording rather than clearly specifying a pipe-name algorithm.

The documented blacklist ignores selected output property names and defaults to an empty array, while ignore controls whether an output is ignored during tests and defaults to false; neither is documented as a destination-write isolation mechanism.

The test guide defaults to /pipes/<my-pipe>/entities and describes endpoint selection as a published /publishers/<my-pipe>/<endpoint-type> read that requires the pipe to publish the chosen endpoint; expected files can be XML as well as default JSON.

Bound parameters in test configuration are documented to work only with published endpoints, default to an empty object, and support separate test files for parameter combinations such as comparing /publishers/foo/xml?my-param=A with foo-A.xml and the B variant with foo-B.xml.

Stage selection defaults to sink, but the local-test table spells intermediate stages before-transform/after-transform while the public entities API spells them before-transforms/after-transforms; the documentation does not establish client aliases for the difference.

One authored test example sets endpoint=json and stage=source but describes an entities-route read, contradicting the guide's general published-endpoint rule and leaving route precedence for that combination uncertain.

The authored foo.test.json example is not directly valid JSON because it contains a shell prompt and lacks a comma after file, and the parameter examples wrap shell transcripts and separate objects in surrounding braces.

The local-test guide says internal properties other than _id and _deleted are removed and entities with _deleted=false are removed, but this is an unverified, suspicious client-normalization statement because Sesam deletion tracking documents _deleted=true for deleted entities.

The inspected local-testing guide does not specify sorting, comparison tolerances, or a complete normalization algorithm, and its client behavior descriptions are external handoffs rather than an inspected implementation.
Service API paths are relative to the instance's API base, which for a cloud instance is typically https://instance-guid.sesam.cloud/api.
The client setup requires a personal subscription and a JWT, with the subscription URL available under the subscription name and JWT generation under Settings > Subscription > JWT.

The documented local test command is sesam -vv test, and the test model runs non-output pipes until their queues have no remaining entities before comparing endpoint output with expected results, rather than starting every pipe only once.

The local guide documents notification of invalid/missing endpoint tests, an all-passed message on success, and failed-test/pipe identification with expected-versus-received comparison on failure; it describes support for updating intended expected outputs but gives no update-results command.

CI requires a designated testing node, runs the same configuration tests as personal testing under CI orchestration, requires successful tests for validation, and recommends peer approval before PR merge; small test data usually permits a smaller node than production.
CI tests against a shared node must be serialized because the client overwrites configuration, causing overlapping tests to fail or not finish.

The documented Jenkins template uses a Kubernetes client container, disableConcurrentBuilds(), a Jenkins credential for the CI JWT, version verification, and a test step exporting NODE/JWT and running from node with -print-scheduler-log; its container-build example pins client version 1.16.1.
The Azure DevOps example downloads the sesam_cli_version release, verifies the CLI version, exports node/node_jwt into NODE/JWT, and runs .././sesam -vv test  -print-scheduler-log from node.

The Azure guide pairs trigger:none with branch build policies, one minimum reviewer, and linked work items on develop/master, and separately instructs disabling parallel builds and queuing the second build, illustrating a Limit=DisAbleParallel capability and matching pool demand.

The configuration API scopes GET/PUT /config to the default empty config-group, GET/PUT /config/{config-group} to the named group, and GET/PUT /config-all to all groups; the PUT operations overwrite the complete configuration in their scope.

Individual pipe/system configuration endpoints express group membership through metadata.$config-group, whereas group-upload endpoints select the group through the URL, with no explicit group placing components in the default group.
force=true on PUT /config and PUT /config-all forces acceptance of configuration errors and best-effort application; the API describes this as rarely a good idea.
The documented GitHub Autodeployer periodically checks repository configuration for changes, can select a tag or branch, and uses the branch setting with a default of master when no tag is specified.

The autodeployer documentation warns that deployment overwrites existing pipes and systems and removes node pipe/system configurations absent from the selected repository branch; the guide hands implementation/configuration details to an external repository rather than specifying the API or config-group handling.

Automatic deployment is optional and the guide cautions that business-critical installations often need release-timing control; the autodeployer only deploys configuration and does not start or reset pipes, leaving required actions manual.

The deployment guide proposes replacing CI test steps with release-parameterized deployment steps in Jenkins/Azure but delegates exact client parameters to client documentation, while the client page explicitly forbids production-subscription use.

Pipes can become out of sync after configuration changes, dataset deletion/recreation, source truncation, backup restoration, new joins/pipe inputs, or deletion of datasets used by hops, requiring reprocessing to restore correct output.
The default reprocessing_policy is continue: the pipe keeps processing without an automatic reset despite desynchronization factors, and the feature guide says affected datasets are tracked.

With reprocessing_policy=automatic, the pipe detects desynchronization and resets/reprocesses inputs, normally with a full rescan but in some situations with a partial rewind; this is pipe/service behavior rather than an autodeployer action.
Reprocessing policy can be set per pipe or as the service-wide default global_defaults.reprocessing_policy, whose documented default is continue.

The pump API separates starting a normal run, starting a rescan unless already running, and reset-rescan, which makes the next rescan restart at the source beginning instead of resuming an interrupted rescan.

This repository's PR workflow installs documentation tools/dependencies and runs make html; the Makefile uses Sphinx with SPHINXOPTS defaulting to -W and generates contract documents for the HTML target, not node-backed Sesam client tests.
The README's documentation preview workflow uses make html and _build/html/index.html, with SPHINXOPTS= make html_no_saas as an alternative preview command.

The repository's master-push workflow builds and publishes a documentation container and deploys the docs Container App; neither that workflow nor the PR build workflow invokes the Sesam client to validate integration fixtures or drain pipe queues.
